classification.difficultyReason: Use the supplied secant substitution, recognise tan²θ=sec²θ−1, back-substitute and determine the integration constant from f(3)=0.

content.prompt: Find the equation of $y=f(x)$ if $f'(x)=\dfrac{\sqrt{x^2-9}}x$ and $f(3)=0$. Use $x=3\sec\theta$.

answer.worked:
We are trying to find $f(x)=\displaystyle\int f'(x)\,dx=\int\dfrac{\sqrt{x^2-9}}x\,dx$.

Let $x=3\sec\theta$, with $0\leq\theta<\dfrac\pi2$. Then $dx=3\sec\theta\tan\theta\,d\theta$.

$$\begin{aligned}\sqrt{x^2-9}&=\sqrt{9\sec^2\theta-9}\\&=\sqrt{9\tan^2\theta}\\&=3\tan\theta.\end{aligned}$$

Also simplify
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=\frac{\sqrt{x^2-9}}x\\&=\frac{3\tan\theta}{3\sec\theta}\\&=\sin\theta.\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}f(x)&=\int\frac{\sqrt{x^2-9}}x\,dx\\&=\int\sin\theta\cdot3\sec\theta\tan\theta\,d\theta\\&=3\int\tan^2\theta\,d\theta\\&=3\int(\sec^2\theta-1)\,d\theta\\&=3(\tan\theta-\theta)+C.\end{aligned}$$

Here $\tan\theta=\dfrac{\sqrt{x^2-9}}3$ and $\theta=\sec^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac x3\right)$, where $\sec^{-1}$ denotes inverse secant. Hence
$$f(x)=\sqrt{x^2-9}-3\sec^{-1}\!\left(\frac x3\right)+C.$$

Substitute $f(3)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}0&=0-3(0)+C\\C&=0.\end{aligned}$$

Therefore $f(x)=\sqrt{x^2-9}-3\sec^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac x3\right)$ on the branch $x\geq3$.
